“It’s what she does,” Iroh said sourly. His body was warm, comfortable, which helped; the rest of Zuko that wasn’t touching his uncle was so cold but Iroh was hot, familiar, the scent of jasmine and other herbs still so strong, like he was made of tea, like a gigantic cozy human teapot.

Sokka looked back, frowning, at Iroh. His eyes softened when they reached Zuko. “Then *why* would you…” he said, his voice trailing off.

Zuko blinked at Sokka, and for one moment Sokka just wasn’t there, which was odd, and instead he saw Azula, her head turned slightly, eyes also wide in concern, and then Sokka was back. His heart beat just a bit faster. That hadn’t been pleasant, none of this was pleasant, like he was teetering over the edge of a dream.

“Family isn’t an easy thing to cut away,” Iroh said quietly, his hold on Zuko’s side tightening, “even when they are a rope around your neck. You have a sister yourself, don’t you?”

Sokka nodded.

“How much would it take for you to truly give up on her? To lose all hope?”

Sokka frowned harder, but his eyes widened, worried. “I get it,” he said quietly.

“Do you…” Iroh had stopped, and Zuko was focused on his shoes and missed something, and a moment later Sokka was on Zuko’s right, holding onto his arm to help. “To let go of family is no easy task. It was a long time before I saw my brother for the man he was; even when he took everything away from me.”

“Your brother is the Fire Lord,” Sokka said seriously, “Zuko mentioned that.”

“That he is,” Iroh said, “and despite knowing, in my heart, it took me witnessing with my own eyes as my brother did something truly unforgivable before I realized who he truly was.”

“Was it… the scar?”

Zuko closed his eyes.

“You don’t miss much,” Iron sounded impressed. “Yes. It was. After what my brother had done, in front of men and women of the court I respected, a heinous act to his own son… the day dawned on the Fire Nation. As all days of my life had before. If such a day could be normal, if the spirits did not rise up in retaliation to so great a wrong, I realized my family- my *nation*, had lost Agni’s light long ago. It was something I think I knew before, I *should have* known before, but had never let myself understand. How deep the darkness of war had spread. To stop the war from inside its walls wasn’t good enough any longer. I had to leave.” The tunnel out had grown steeper, for several more yards ahead.

“You’re an interesting young man, Sokka of the Southern Water Tribe,” Iroh’s tone was different, not much warning from the somber notes of only a moment before until he changed to something jovial.

Sokka leaned forward, to look at Iroh past Zuko’s head. “I am?” He asked.

Zuko liked that they were both here, liked… them, but he wasn’t exactly sure how he felt about the two of them *talking* to each other. Especially now, when focus on reality was growing harder and harder as unconsciousness kept tugging at his mind and he wasn’t sure he could keep track of what they were saying.

Iroh grunted, guiding the three of them forward. “Seeing *you* kissing my nephew was almost as surprising as him,” Iroh pointed out.

“*Uncle*,” Zuko muttered, but he wasn’t sure either of them could hear it, he was barely audible under his breath. He swallowed, trying to get enough moisture in his throat to find his voice again.

“Uh… why?” Sokka asked, raising an eyebrow.

Iroh chuckled. “You haven’t forgotten I was there, have you? When you received the *blessing* of the new moon spirit?”

Sokka coughed so loudly Zuko winced.

“A pretty girl, that was,” Iroh continued pleasantly, pausing only to encourage Zuko over a ridge in the tunnel, “Princess of the North, if my memory is correct.”

“Y- Yue,” Sokka sputtered, “I, she was- *yeah*.”

*Princess*, what was with this talk about a *princess*, Azula was already *gone*. Zuko’s headache was back, full force, encouraged from how tense he felt between his eyes as he tried to keep his mind on the task at hand.

“Curious,” Iroh muttered, sounding suspicious. Zuko couldn’t fathom *why*.

This would be a lot easier for him if the two of them would stay *quiet*, let Zuko just worry about staying upright and not whether or not Sokka and his uncle could get along.

“C- curious?” Sokka repeated, his voice getting higher.

“Mhm,” Iroh confirmed.

Zuko wondered if that made sense to Sokka, it certainly didn’t for him.

“Sokka of the Southern Water Tribe,” Iroh said, with a tone of voice Zuko knew was trouble, because Iroh appeared to be amusing himself, “what would you say *are* your intentions with my nephew?”

“I-“ Sokka squeaked, “Am I supposed to have *intentions*?”

“Every action has an intention,” Iroh explained, “whether it's as minor as a single step through this dark tunnel… or kissing my nephew.”

“Ah, oh, *well*!” Sokka coughed, “That’s-"

“The route is level here,” Iroh told him, “it would be best for you to walk ahead again.”

Sokka was gone, his hands left Zuko’s side. And Zuko’s heart skipped. He could see the mask in front of him, the Dark Water Spirit, grinning in front of his face with an eye scarred from a boomerang. It wanted him, wanted to *take*, wanted Zuko to put it back on and fall away into his role, to take everything away and it wasn’t *fair*- this wasn’t what she would have *wanted* for him-what would his mother say? What would she think of him? If she had seen everything Zuko had done since she’d gone?

“-son?” Sokka’s voice, a few yards ahead, snapped Zuko back to the moment.

“During my siege of Ba Sing Se.”

“*Your* siege?!”

“Yes.”

Zuko looked down at his stomach, black fabric ripped and poking out of careful white bandages, red around his center. His right hand, hanging listlessly to his side, was covered in sticky, dark liquid. As his head hung down, while he looked, beads of sweat dropped from his forehead onto the ground below, ground that inched away as Iroh guided him forward.

It had been *his* turn to lie down injured in a cave, hurt by someone he once cared for and nursed back to health by others who cared for him. Zuko really had a lot in common with Jet, he mused, feeling a pang in his chest. He hoped Jet was recovering well, hoped his Freedom Fighters kept him safe as he rested; he hoped they’d see each other again, someday, on friendlier terms.

“I’m sorry,” Sokka was saying.

“There is no call for an apology on your part, Sokka of the Water Tribe, but I appreciate it nonetheless.” Iroh’s voice was warm in Zuko’s mind, relaxing, like the heat of a gentle fire on a chilly day.

---

“I’ll stay with him.”

*What*? What happened? Zuko wanted o sit up, but there was an arm wrapped around his stomach holding him down. He blinked, trying to get his eyes to focus.

Time had just… skipped. He hadn’t even been aware of it, there hadn’t been any dreams, all of the sudden the world was bright outside and he was lying down in dirt.

“You can firebend, I’m a guy with a boomerang without a boomerang so-"

“I suppose you’re right.”

“Yeah. You help my sister, I’ll watch your nephew, it seems fair to me.”

His lungs were heavy, it took a considerable amount more effort than usual to breathe and Zuko found himself concentrating on that for a while as he tried to make sense of everything. He felt so light, like he could float, and at the same time even twitching his hand seemed like too difficult a task. He was on the ground, yes, on the ground, and… and…

Something cool pressed onto his forehead, and Zuko raised his eyes upward to look.

Sokka was looking down at him. He smiled.

Zuko was tucked against a garden wall, Sokka leaning his back to it, lying down half-hidden beside some ornamental plants on a raised platform. There were noises, like a fight or something happening, but extremely distant, and from the way Sokka’s shoulders were relaxed Zuko knew that the fight was far enough away from them both. They were safe, for the moment, Zuko’s head and shoulders pulled up to rest in Sokka’s lap.

Sokka had a rag in his hand and he lifted it again, dripping some of the water from the jug he was carrying onto it before returning it to Zuko’s forehead. “Are you with us again?” Sokka asked him, “You faded for awhile there.”

Zuko tried to swallow, his throat was extremely dry and his tongue was heavy, but he nodded.

“This came fast that’s-" Sokka frowned, for a second, before letting himself smile again. Zuko wasn’t sure now how authentic Sokka’s expression was, but it was still nice to see. “Just tell me if you see any dancing mushrooms, okay?”

Had Sokka actually said that or was Zuko’s mind playing tricks on him again? He probably had, Sokka said a lot of weird things.

Sokka looked up, toward the source of the noise. “Don’t know what’s up with Aang,” he mused, “or how much danger they’re in- your sister she, she had us in the pot before we even noticed. Now it’s boiling all at once.”

Zuko watched him, his stomach hurt, as expected, but there was an ache in his chest the longer he looked at Sokka in this moment.

“We’re going to lose this city,” Sokka said quietly, “might have lost the invasion plans, and I guess we lost the Avatar State too.” He was looking away, passed where Zuko could see, but despite his words he didn’t seem sad or even angry. “We’ll figure it out. Find *some* kind of answer, I know it,” his eyes hardened, determined, “we lost Ba Sing Se and Omashu but… I know Aang wouldn’t be here if it wasn’t fate. What would be the point, after a hundred years? I have just as much faith in him as my sister, even if I’m more realistic about it. I just wish… wish all of this wasn’t so hard.” Sokka sighed, and looked down at Zuko. “Hi.”

Zuko blinked up at him for a moment, and smiled. “*Hi*,” he said back, his voice choking slightly from how dry and hoarse he was.

Sokka immediately brought the water jug up for him, uncorking it and bringing it toward his mouth. Saving perhaps the last bit of his dignity though, Zuko managed to grab it himself. He raised it, hand trembling, and drank.

It was *excellent*, the water, cold and refreshing as it slipping down his throat. Zuko barely swallowed as he washed it down, as much as he could manage before he started coughing.

“I can’t believe I’m complaining to *you*, sorry,” Sokka mumbled as he set the water jug down beside them.

“I *think*,” Zuko said, painfully but his mouth twitching into a grin, “you have… *more* right to complain.”

“*Really*?” Sokka asked him, raising an eyebrow, “And who is the one with a *stab* wound and a fever?”

“I grew up in a palace,” Zuko reminded him, raising his trembling hand just enough to push his knuckles against Sokka’s arm.

Sokka snorted. “Yeah, with *your* dad,” he said, smirking. He leaned forward, his head directly over Zuko’s line of sight so he was eclipsing the light, draped over by shadow in a way that was comforting. A way that seemed to belong only to the two of them despite being outside in the royal gardens, exposed to the world, but together they weren’t. They were alone. “You telling me you didn’t have it rough?” He asked, his eyes twinkling.

Zuko swallowed. “I… did have to work in a teashop,” he rasped.

“Hm,” Sokka rolled his eyes, “well, *I’ve* had this crick in my neck from sleeping on Appa’s saddle, for *months*.”

“Stung by ant-bees,” Zuko mumbled.

“I’ve had a rock in my shoe this whole time,” Sokka countered with a grin, “literally. Since I fell into this cave.”

Zuko wanted to chuckle, though his body was so tired it came out only as a quick exhale. “My first boyfriend tried to kill me,” he said.

“My first girlfriend turned into the *moon*.”

Zuko blinked at him. “Oh.”

“Crap,” Sokka said with amusement, “did I win?”

“Is *that* why…” Zuko started to say, before he was coughing again. His chest lurched forward, stomach tightened and sent pain coursing through him, but Sokka grabbed his shoulders and held him down. The coughing fit had him light-headed again, to the point when everything grew dizzy. When worst of it was over, his body still trembling, Sokka raised the water jug again to his mouth. Zuko drank, not caring anymore for dignity, as the water soothed his throat.

“I,” Sokka was saying, continuing on as if nothing had happened, “don’t think I can picture you working in a *tea shop*. Though, ask me a couple months ago and I wouldn’t have been able to picture you with hair either.”

“I can still... the dress,” Zuko mumbled.

Sokka’s eyes widened as he stared at Zuko. “Um.”

“And the makeup,” Zuko continued hoarsely, “Kyoshi Island.”

“Oh, uh, *well*,” Sokka lifted a hand to rub the back of his neck, “I was training with the Kyoshi warriors. It was- I mean, I *wore* the dress, yeah. Surprisingly comfortable except for, well, the armor.” He coughed, loudly, muttering into his fist, “I can’t believe you remember that.”

“I,” Zuko started to say, but his stomach tightened as a wave of pain hit with no warning. Burns were like that, they throbbed like a heartbeat where it didn’t belong, still and sizzling until they struck, taking away all breath and sense. He grinded his teeth together, swallowing the groan.

Sokka took his hands, holding them tight, as Zuko waited for it to stop. For the pain to lessen only… it wasn’t. It was sticking, ripping into him, *the burn that his uncle-*

“Hey, uh, I remember more now,” Sokka said, his voice tight, breaking through Zuko’s headache to fill his mind, “in Liudong River? I hadn’t- I didn’t *forget* it before, you know, I just hadn’t thought about it. That’s all.”

Zuko’s face was forced tight, barely managing to keep his seeing eye open. Water built along the edges of his already limited vision but he forced himself to focus, keep his eyes on Sokka, *pay* *attention*.

“How I pulled you out of the water, remember?” Sokka continued, his words growing more and more rushed, “and then you returned the favor, knocking us out from under the tank? I thought about that a lot, actually, after I found out who you were- after I *saw* you without the mask. Just… trying to figure you out. You really didn’t make it easy.”

Zuko took a shaking breath in through his nose. He wanted to talk, more than anything, but he *couldn’t*.

“And, and-" Sokka adjusted his hands over Zuko’s, pulling them up to his chest, “you saving those people during the attack, pulling *me* out, and- bringing me breakfast. It was a good breakfast.”

Zuko nodded. He found just enough strength in his fingers to squeeze Sokka’s hands back.

“Oh man, uh, listening me when I talked about missing home, and my dad, a- and the tribe, how you,” Sokka looked upward toward the sky, blinking rapidly, before bringing his eyes back to Zuko. “Then, when you could have had a chance to get more information you, you just wanted to sit with me. Doing nothing. And how nice that was. And how Jet said you saved him, then you found Appa, I just- it’s like you were half bad and half good all the time, and you couldn’t figure it out, and it’s- it’s *really* just, it’s,” his voice cracked, “it’s *not fair* that you- that the second you do something *right* this happens.” Sokka’s mouth was twitching downward hard, almost seemingly like it hurt how much he was attempting to force a smile.

Zuko, despite everything, relaxed his jaw just enough to talk. His voice sounded pathetic, grating and weak, but he was at least able enough to say, “Bad luck.”

Sokka stared at him for a moment, and then chuckled. “Bad luck,” he whispered. “You mean *you* have bad luck?”

Zuko nodded, smiled at him though his face wasn’t cooperating enough; it was likely more of a grimace, but Sokka still seemed to like it. His vision hadn’t gotten any better but he could feel Sokka raise his hands, the press of a mouth into one of his thumbs. *Good*, that was good.

“I think,” Sokka said, his voice choked, “we are owed a *lot* of luck. For the… teashop and the rock in my shoe. Right?”

There was a shadow, over Sokka’s shoulder. For a moment, an utterly ridiculous moment, Zuko thought it was his uncle until she stepped closer.

She had a darkness across her face, clinging to her shape like a mask, as she stood over the both of them, tall and imposing but soft despite the lines of her regal coat.

“Right? Spirits?” Sokka said, throwing his head up and talking a bit louder, “You owe us some luck this time so just…” Zuko’s hands were lifted higher, pressed against Sokka’s eyes, as Sokka whispered, “make Katara hurry. *Please*.”

She knelt down, raising a delicate hand upward toward his face, and though he couldn’t see hers Zuko just knew, with an ache in his chest, that she was frowning. A shade, perched on the edge of reality, and she couldn’t be there, couldn’t *be* the way she seemed, because the woman he saw was a giant, far bigger than she should. She was as large, compared to him, as she was in Zuko’s memories, but that was six long years ago and Zuko had grown.

“Oh, Zuko,” she whispered, her voice sharp as a knife, echoing through his mind. She lowered her hand just enough to place it over his scar. “Your father is never going to hurt you. You think I’d allow it?”

“You died,” Zuko said to her.

Her hand was suddenly taken over by another, wisped away, as Sokka lurched forward to grab Zuko’s face. He was leaning forward, suddenly *right there*, bursting into Zuko’s vision like a light. “Who are you talking to?!” Sokka demanded, as she loomed over his shoulder. “Hey, hey, look at *me.*”

Zuko wanted to look at him, he did, but she was *there*, in whatever form she’d come to him as. It was *her* . He knew it, he *knew* , he could feel her, he felt- he felt-

“Zuko, Zuko, *please,* okay- god you’re burning up this is- *shit* , you-"

“*You*,” the shade leaned forward, creating words out of thin air despite her absence of a face, “You don't *look* like my son.”

Zuko’s heart was racing now, as it had been before but now it felt unnatural. The beating of a war drum growing ever faster, relentless inside his heart, *pounding* and cracking like a snare.

He knew Sokka was there, tangentially, he could feel the cool rag coming back to wipe at the sweat on his face, but so was *she*, and this wasn’t a phantom Zuko was sure he wanted to *fight*. Why did she have to be so dark? Why had she come to him like this, wrapped in shadow, intimidating, when all he wanted was to see her eyes light up again as he raced into her arms?

“You,” Zuko struggled, as his heart was racing so was his breathing, so staggered, “don’t look like,” he had to *try*, to speak, to say *something* to her, “my mother.”

“*Hey*!” Sokka yelled, and then his face was even closer, eyebrows furrowed tight, eyes flashing their brilliant blue, his mouth curled into a scowl full of teeth, “'*Look'* at me, okay! No one is there! Look at my face!”

His eye flickered away from her to Sokka for a split second, and when they came back to her she was still there. That was good- that was- his stomach twisting, and it *hurt*, everything hurt, Zuko focused his gaze on Sokka, careful as he did to be aware of the looming shadow behind him.

“Zuko,” Sokka said, then more forcefully, “*Zuko.*”

“‘S a nice face,” Zuko mumbled, “your face.”

“Listen you have to- *uh…* ” Sokka blinked at him for a moment, then shook his head, “ *thanks*, listen you have to stay awake until Katara gets here, okay?”

Her head surged slightly closer in his view, the deep wells where her eyes would be hovering beside Sokka’s ear. “Yeah,” Zuko whispered.

“Okay, okay, I- hey!” Sokka managed, with what appeared to be considerable effort, to smile, “Have you- I haven’t told you how I earned my mark, it’s ice dodging, this very cool tradition, so you… you want me to talk?”

Zuko nodded at him, which he shouldn’t have, it sent a wave of nausea through him. It was enough though, for Sokka to start in on a story that Zuko could barely pay attention to.

It was nice to hear his voice though, the somewhat hypnotizingly rhythmic stops and starts as Sokka interrupted one thought with another. A story that began on the shores of the earth kingdom shifted instantly to explain part of Sokka’s childhood in the ice covered world in the south, meandering all around a subject like a coin rotating along a narrowing bowl, the end destination the only thing to keep each tangent held together.

Words, Sokka’s voice, his hands carefully holding Zuko’s head upward, one thumb quietly brushing under Zuko’s unscarred ear like Sokka wasn’t even aware he was doing it. Zuko could focus, just enough, on the light surrounding Sokka’s hair as he leaned down over him, how it left a glow along the edges of his frame, how despite the shade leering behind him that halo of sunshine was uninterrupted, giving Sokka a golden appearance as he simultaneously explained why he had once thought digging a fishhook out of his thumb with another fishhook had seemed like a good idea at the time.

It was so hard to force himself awake, every blink held the risk of his eye closing permanently to allow him to drift off into the dream that loomed overhead, only waiting. A sleep Zuko desperately wanted, more than anything, as it was offering the slim possibility of seeing his mother’s face again.

Sokka’s words, and the warmth of his hands on Zuko’s sweating, freezing skin, washed over him like ceaseless waves on the ocean but also unobserved or examined. So much so that Zuko missed entirely as Sokka’s voice shifted, yelling, to questions that were given foreign answers, having no idea that anything had changed until a pair of hands gripped him from the armpits and was yanking him to his feet.

“Careful!” Sokka yelled.

“I got him, hurry-"

“Toph! No, you *don’t*!”

“Why not?”

“Just-"

Somehow, despite the fever and the pain and Zuko’s dwindling grasp on reality, he had enough of his consciousness left to be thoroughly embarrassed as he was handled and shoved into the air like a limp doll. He was caught by the arm, had a face full of what had to be fur, before being dragged upward over and into a rough woven saddle. His body dropped onto a smaller body, one that almost fell over from his weight, as he collapsed to the ground with half his chest and an arm being lifted slightly into the air.

The process of recovering from all of *that* was almost too much for him to take. His stomach was a raging pit of pain, his head pounded ceaselessly along with the shouting of several voices near him, and a sinking unreality grew even sharper as a deep, hollowness filled his body along with the rush of an unnatural breeze.

“*Katara-"*

Zuko smelled Iroh before he could recognize the hands that were drawing him closer, lifting Zuko’s head and shoulders into a lap. Zuko’s neck dropped his head, unable to lift himself up any longer, not even that, but his uncle’s hand brushed against his hair and held Zuko’s head upright, pillowed on his wide stomach.

Zuko opened his eyes for a split second, saw five chaotic figures and several colors of fur as the walls of a building rushed passed him unnaturally quick, at an impossible angle, and someone screamed as a boulder came careening in their direction. He slammed his eyes shut.

As he fought the nausea, while the wildly flying *beast* dodged unseen obstacles in the sky and Zuko was frankly sure he’d never felt worse in his *life*, Iroh gripped him tightly in place, his hold on Zuko as unshakeable as stone. Zuko could feel the sensation of falling, over and over, as he was losing his battle with sleep and the bison kept going *up and up and up*, but his uncle was there. Iroh wasn’t going to let him go.

His uncle’s stomach moved, out and in, exaggerated breathing that brought Zuko’s head with it, and eventually Zuko managed to mimic him. Just breathe. Everything was breathing, breath was life and fire; Zuko could handle that, and only that, just bring in air through his lungs and let it out.

“I can’t- *what is wrong with you*?! How could you bring *him*?!”

“I know! Okay!”

“Apparently not!”

“Just *listen to me*!”

He had to look, even keeping his eye closed as much as possible, forcing himself to see even a sliver of the world around him. But as everything came, painstakingly slowly, into view and Zuko made the connections from one thing to another, the edge of a saddle, a furry creature beside a man in expensive robes, a young girl standing, giant horns and an orange figure in between, and two bodies in blue on his right, kneeling close together- real, they were all real, there was no more shade, no more black figure looming overhead with her hand reached out to him, she was-

She was *gone*.

Zuko was shivering now, he wasn’t sure he was sweating anymore, he hoped the water building up in his eyes, sliding down his cheeks went unnoticed but he wasn’t sure they did.

“Why are you *hesitating*- you *have to-!*”

“Sokka! After everything he *did*-!”

“Yes!”

Stop spinning. The world had to stop spinning. *Please*.

“Uh, guys-"

“What is wrong with you?!”

“Stop *arguing* with me and just do it! He’s hurt!”

“I am *going* to! I’m not going to just *leave someone to*-!”

“Then hurry up!”

“I can’t until Appa is flying steady, I could hurt him worse, Sokka!”

“Oh, well- that makes sense!”

“Of course it does!”

“Okay!”

“*Good!"*

He really… just wanted to sleep. Iroh holding him so tightly, as the words shouted into the air barely managed to be heard over the rapid fluttering of a breeze as the creature climbed into the sky, the way Zuko felt like he couldn’t move a single muscle in his body, it was the deepest ache for sleep. Every part of him wanted to reach out and slip into a dream, even the bit of him that was awake, that could think, wanted to find *her* again.

His uncle’s hand on his head swept through his sweaty hair, pinching it slightly just enough to force Zuko back when he started to drift, as if Iroh could read his mind and knew when Zuko was slipping.

He might have felt every second as acutely as possible, but as soon as Zuko opened his eyes to Katara manipulating water over his stomach all the memory of the waiting was promptly forgotten. She carefully brought a hand down, delicate, as the water seeped through the wet bandages and absorbed it’s way into his skin.

Sokka was hovering over her shoulder, his eyes focused intently on what Katara was doing. One hand raised upward to grip his sister’s shoulder as Katara’s face furrowed in concentration. She had dirt swept across her face, part of her shirt was torn but otherwise seemed to have come through whatever fight unscathed. The other girl, the earthbender, appeared the same, uninjured but clearly shaken; she was bent down on the saddle, both hands touching the leather, her head toward the ground and one ear tilted in Zuko’s direction. Beside her, for a reason Zuko was too tired to bother figuring out, was a well-dressed man apparently in his twenties and some large, blankly blinking, subspecies of platypus-bear with a weird pinched face.

Katara suddenly sharply raised her head and met Zuko’s eyes.

“I know,” Toph said, her voice barely audible over the rushing of wind, “I can feel it too.”

“Feel what?” Sokka asked, turning his head sharply to the other girl.

“I-" Katara stared at Zuko, her blue eyes widening. Zuko was struck by how alike she and Sokka looked, their twin eyes and similar features, the same way their mouths tightened when they were scared.

Iroh’s stomach shook, as Zuko heard his uncle’s breathing behind his ear grow staggered.

“*Toph*,” Sokka said, a tone to his voice that sent a shiver through Zuko’s chest, “you feel *what*?”

Katara stared at Zuko, and he could practically see her mind racing behind her eyes. Turmoil, an extremely familiar emotion, chasing each thought and fighting over every word, coming to an eventual, hard-won conclusion. She turned her head to Sokka, and Zuko couldn’t see the rest, if they said anything quietly to each other or if they just looked at each other and *knew* , but when Katara’s gaze came back to Zuko her jaw was set and determination flooded over her expression.

She reached into her shirt, bowing her head slightly, and lifted up a vial strapped by a delicate chain around her neck. It seemed important, significant, small patterns around the little container in a beautiful display, a stopper at the top made of some brilliant light blue material that shimmered in the sun, carved into a waning crescent moon.

“Thank you,” Iroh whispered, his voice rumbling, cracking with emotion, as Katara brought water out of the vial, circling it in the air as it sparkled with unknown light.

She was saving his life, Zuko knew it, and while a part of him that was still angry felt he deserved this, for betraying his people and joining their side, the part of him that had a lot more reason knew he had no right to ask for this, from Katara especially.

Yet, despite that, she brought her hand down softly, easing the luminescent water into his body.

It was a *sigh*. The water easing into his wound and bringing back feelings that had gone away, tingling, no amount of pain, only the most pleasant of sensations. Like a long awaited cool breeze on the hottest of summer days.

“Will he-?” Sokka’s voice, he was talking, saying something, more people were talking, they all began buzzing with words that tripped over one another, tumbling into Zuko’s head as nonsense.

Iroh’s hand on Zuko’s forehead lowered, slipping down over his eyes. “You can sleep now,” his uncle whispered gently, “it’s alright.”

Zuko closed his eyes and began to dream.

## Chapter 24: Reignition

He should dance. Zuko is *dressed* for a dance. That’s what they do, the men like him, with painted faces and scrolls full of jokes hidden in the pockets of their feminine robes, they dance and they entertain and they mingle around the crowd to ensure everyone keeps up the good humor, encouraging drinking, encouraging laughter, encouraging the world to laugh at them; Zuko’s dress is green like the colors of Ba Sing Se, his face is painted and though he can’t see it he knows, he *knows*.

He stands on the tournament ground, as the flags above a jeering crowd portray the sun and a flag of war, of honor on the line, and they are dressed, the crowd, in the way they were on that day; he sees faces he knows, ones who once lavished him with compliments realizing now all the energy was wasted on the wrong child, the faces of his teachers as their expression sours, knowing that the prestigious position of teaching the crown prince had *not*, in fact, been as great a position as they could have received, he sees Zhao, who used to bow at his feet and request Zuko pass along messages to his father, the greatest sycophant Zuko had ever met, as unbridled glee covers his face, unmasked now in Zuko’s presence as he would be for the rest of his life, he sees Ty Lee and Mai’s parents, people he knew for so long, from the time he was small, and he knows they’re confused, somewhere, behind the stoicism of nobility, expressions of stone that give away nothing, not even a sliver of concern for a boy who once played with their daughters, and there is Azula, smiling, watching him with piercing eyes, enjoying this, enjoying the sight, enjoying the thrill as Zuko is humiliated, the way she does, the look on her face one of triumph, and he sees as well the face of his uncle. There is only one person Zuko *wants* to look, only one pair of eyes he is sure he could find some comfort inside, he wants to see something, *anything* , other than the blank faces, the smiling faces, the *laughing* faces; but Iroh has turned away.

His father takes his steps up onto the platform, he is so very tall, so very strong, and the sight of him, as always, fills Zuko as much longing as it does fear. Ozai compels Zuko to dance, as the world laughs, as they stare at the taikomochi in front of them, as they wait for the jester to entertain; but Zuko doesn’t know how to dance. No one ever taught him how.

---

He felt as he was brought to a bed. Lowered into a pile of warm coverings that smell of leather, and fur tickled the underside of his nose, and before Zuko was awake enough to ask for water to parch his starving throat he sank again into a dream.

---

Zuko can feel the darkness tugging into him, little fingers from tiny creatures, spirits of shame to reach deep into his chest and pull it apart starting at the wound between his ribcage. They want to force him down, deeper, they want him to fall and to break and the hands are sweeping over him like the waves of a dark ocean, like the living water that had pulled Zhao under to drown as Zuko watched, it’s coming to kill him, all these little creatures, and Zuko knows, somehow, that they’ve all come from himself; a death he cultivated in the darkness, in years of holding them back to only let them grow stronger, let them fester. They curl into him now, slicing, biting, so very full of anger at being kept from the light. It isn’t fair, to have kept them hidden for so long, they hate him, deeply, as they multiply to crawl to his face, up to his mouth to slip between teeth, but if they eat his mouth he won’t be able to set them free any longer, he won’t be able to call out their name, truth, to let them out into existence - he only kept them hidden to save his own skin and now the shameful little spirits of dishonor had come to drown him.

Zuko screams, and flails in the dark, and begs them for forgiveness but he knows they can tell, he knows they know he doesn’t *mean* it, that if he had the chance to hide these terrifying truth spirits again he would do so. He’d push them deep in the dark and out of sight, he’d beat them down, he’d crush them into dust if only given the opportunity, so they don’t relent, they eat him away as he reaches out for something, anyone-

A hand grabs his and Zuko pulls it close.

He is sitting on a wagon, one full of supplies and goods, the smell of hay and feathered beasts in the air as somewhere a sheepgoat bleats, and far in the distance the tall walls of Ba Sing Se shiver and sway like an artists painting while Zuko pulls on a calloused hand to lift Sokka up.

The shame is gone. Like a snap of fingers. Only the echoes remain tucked harmlessly away under his stomach, where they might be forever, as Sokka grins and sits down on a crate at his side. Their hands stay clasped together, Sokka’s has dirt under the fingernails and scars on a thumb, and despite how thin he is there’s a strength there from years of work, as the hand holds Zuko’s and holds on tight.

“So,” Sokka asks with a smile, “where are we going?”

This is not how it went. They didn’t choose to run away. They stayed.

“I’d love a place with the ocean. Maybe a little cold.”

This is the simplest solution. The easy one. Everything is solved, if they only take this path. It’s a world where Zuko is not the prince who terrorized Sokka’s people, where neither of them need to fight a war that’s older than they are by six of their lifetimes; they could forget, as they lived this unexamined life together, that Zuko is half a monster and Sokka once wished he was dead.

“Halong Bin,” Zuko whispers to him, the map of the Earth Kingdom bright with possibility in his mind. It is cold there, low on the world, cold weather crops and fish, but the appeal was the mountains. People could be lost forever in the mountains.

The little spirits began to return, slipping into life from underneath his turned arm, multitudes of them, crawling skin leeches and yet Sokka doesn’t notice. Even as they cross the threshold of their held hands. Zuko tries to open his mouth to warn him but he isn’t able to speak of them, he can only watch as his infestation spreads.

“You would take me away?” Sokka asks him, his voice loud as if it was spoken directly into Zuko’s ears, “You would steal me from my family?”

“Yes,” Zuko replies.

“My father’s only son? You would take that from him,” Sokka asks, as the creatures Zuko had made advance along his arm, “when your family already took his wife?”

“I would,” Zuko promises, “I’d take care of you. I’d never let you want for anything.”

“And if I wanted to go home?” Sokka asks, his words punctuated with each syllable as the pain in Zuko grew to cover Sokka’s chest, to slither up his neck, “Could you give me that?”

“No,” Zuko admits to him, quietly, embarrassed.

They were sinking into Zuko’s stomach now, deeper and deeper, as the shame creatures grew across Sokka’s face, faster and faster, leaving only his eyes shining out in the darkness. “Is this how you want me?” Sokka asks, “Is this how you’d like me to be? Hidden away in the dark like you?”

“No,” Zuko breaths, “no.”

“But you *asked*.”

“I would,” Zuko feels his words swallowed up by wind, by himself, by the fading of the reality around him, “I wanted this, I didn’t think-"

“You weren’t thinking about me, were you?” Sokka asks, “It was only you, wasn’t it? You were only thinking about you?”

He stares at him, a Sokka overtaken by Zuko’s own creatures, and his heart aches. It is too much to see, too much to feel, too much to hate, but Zuko cannot close his eyes. “I would never have forced you,” Zuko says, his only, his *last*, defence for his honor in this exchange.

“But you *asked*,” Sokka reminds him, “and it wasn’t a fair thing to ask of me.”

“It wasn’t,” Zuko whispers, earnestly, as repentant as a pilgrim bowing before a shrine. “It wasn’t a fair thing to ask.”

Sokka, only recognizable now by his piercing blue eyes, lets go of Zuko’s hand and allows him to sink once more.

---

For some reason, Zuko can still feel the hand in his own. He is sure, too, that the hand is Sokka’s, as the noise of the dream is much louder now. A hand Zuko was certain had let go, to leave him in the dark, but now that it was back he held it tightly.

It was Sokka, Zuko could recognize his hand in his own. Despite how few times they had, in reality, held each others hand, and despite how fleeting those moments had been, each time Zuko had been determined to commit the feeling to memory. And, each time, had been so deeply curious to hold his hand without gloves getting in the way. Wondered what it would be like. He had the answer now, unfortunately, as he could feel sweat all over his palm and the hold was slightly painful to control the shaking of Zuko’s hand. The sentiment was what mattered, though, just knowing Sokka was *there*.

He heard a voice talk and another reply, as a gentle cold substance touched the irritated skin on his stomach, pressing into the wound in a way that only soothed. One familiar voice encouraged another, more irritated one, as the lulling gentle cool of healing water let Zuko relax again.

---

The deck of his ship is cool, as the freezing winds of the south bluster over its metal surface. Unfeeling metal, not like grass, dirt, or sand. Metal can’t remember the feet that step over it, this vessel is an old warship from ages past that has carried hundreds of soldiers across the oceans and yet contains no ghosts, even the dust of men long past has been cleaned away, their ashes forgotten, the echoes of their voice unheard in the cold, unnatural, unstoppable depths of this machine.

The wind whips around him, over his robe, as Zuko stands at the head of the deck and refuses to shiver.

“A man needs his rest,” his uncle tells him from far behind, in that careful way of lying; pretending he is speaking to the air, to himself, but each word meant for Zuko to overhear.

Zuko had refused. Here, in the South Pole, and stayed staring into the dark and the ice until his body was so cold even his inner fire was nothing but an ember. Later, in the North Pole, after Zuko had lost, and lost, and *lost* , after there were more burns on him than he’d bothered to count, after he’d seen a man die, Iroh had said the words again. That time, Zuko had rested.

But this is different. This is a dream. Zuko knows it is a dream, because, as with all dreams but the one, he can see clearly everything in front of him, even the world at his left. There is no scar on his face.

The robe though, it flickers across his body, buffeted by the wind, and Zuko sees the burn on his stomach.

“Prince Zuko,” his uncle says to him, a voice that brings along warmth to Zuko’s chest, “do you still wish me gone?”

Zuko reaches out, his hands clinging tight to the metal walls at the head of the ship. He can’t turn his head around, can’t bring himself to look back at Iroh; his eyes are forced to focus ahead, as his ship barrels through freezing water and chunks of ice, a snowfall of ash blazing the way ahead.

“You wished I would go away so many times,” his uncle is speaking gently, but it *hurts* , it hurts. “You wished your cousin had come back, instead of me-"

Zuko drops his forehead to the cool metal and wants to scream.

“Don’t deny it,” his uncle admonishes him.

“I won’t,” Zuko promises. It’s true. He knows it’s true. Lu Ten, who had been a friend to him, who had extended invitations that allowed Zuko to skip lessons, who had made Ursa proud just with the attention Lu Ten gave to her son; who had promised Zuko a career in the war at his side, who had been there, if only for a short while; Zuko had missed Lu Ten, had wished he’d come home, and hadn’t known Iroh enough to realize what else Zuko would have been missing if the spirits had accepted his request.

“You wished your cousin had returned instead of me,” his uncle says again, as if to twist the knife even deeper, “and you wished your father had been the one to accompany you on this journey.”

“I did,” Zuko apologizes, pressing his forehead harder into the railing of the ship, “I did, I did.”

“How dare you?!” His uncle’s voice cracks, like thunder. “Have I ever raised my hand to you if not to save you? Have I ever asked for anything in return? Have I been anything other than kind?!”

Zuko shakes his head. He hates this dream, somehow even more than the others, hates it as deeply as the ocean before him is deep.

“If your father *had* come with you on this journey, if it *had* been him by your side, would you have had a moment's peace? Any amusement? Any place to let yourself *feel*, to be frustrated, to cry, to scream? Would it not have been *frightening* ?” His uncle was angry, the kind of anger Zuko had only heard him use once in his presence before Zuko’s cowering had caused his uncle to lock that tone away, never to be used on him again. “You would rather have *him*! You would choose *your* *father* over me?”

“Not anymore,” Zuko kneels at the bow of the ship, “not anymore.”

“And *how long* did it take you to learn that lesson! How much of my time did I have to *waste* on *you*?!”

“Too much,” Zuko curls his arms over his scarred stomach. “So much of your time.”

“You took me for granted, you grew *tired* of me, you were disobedient and defiant in my teachings, *over and over again*!” His uncle’s rage matches the cracking of the ice as the ship barrels onward, without ceasing, carving a course of destruction through the water. “I *embarrass* you, don’t I?”

“You have, but you don’t-" Zuko is trying to explain, but his uncle interrupts him without pause and Zuko flinches.

“What *right* does a person *like you* have to be embarrassed of *me*?!” His uncle steps closer, and Zuko can hear the crisp clank of his uncle’s shoes as he draws near, and Zuko bends forward, shaking now from something other than the cold. “You should have *begged* for my wisdom, for my lessons, I am the grandson of Sozin the Great, the Mighty, the Avatar-slayer! I am the son of Azulon, who your own beloved mother dishonorably brought to an end! I am the Dragon of the West! A decorated general! A hero of the people! And who are *you*, Zuko? What have *you* done?”

Zuko raises his shaking hands toward his eyes, to hide behind, but as the pads of his fingers touch his skin he can feel the paint covering his face. He freezes.

“You, who has brought nothing *but* shame to this family! Who cannot complete even the *one task* that was asked of you!” Zuko squeezes his eyes shut, as closed as he can, but this is a dream and it doesn't help; it doesn’t stop him from hearing the words he remembers so well. “A diseased little *thing* in a litter, living on when it would have been better to let the river *take you*! It was barely mercy you were spared as a child, far crueler to allow a disappointment to live!”

He knows that, knows it’s only an echo of words said a long time ago, but it’s wrong, it’s *worse*, to hear *those words* spoken in his uncle’s voice.

“I offered you love and you pushed me away!” His uncle is yelling so loudly, shouting so angrily, so much closer to the front of the ship now, closer *to Zuko*. “I gave you a place to be safe to speak your mind, I offered you my resources and the power of my name as you traveled, I extended to you freedom and you used that to be *disobedient*! Where was the respect *I* was due, Prince Zuko?! Why did you hate the love I had for you?!”

“I don’t-" Zuko tries to say.

“*Speak*!” His uncle orders him.

Zuko curls his body forward into his hands. “I don’t understand it, I don’t know it, I can’t believe-I don’t deserve it-"

“Do you not trust me?!” His uncle hollers.

Zuko shakes his head, over and over and over again, and whispers, “I do.”

“Then *why* do you imagine I would *ever* speak to you *like this*?!”

“I don’t know, I don’t know,” Zuko buries his unscarred, painted face into his hands, “I don’t know.”

“Is *this* who I am?! Even *now*, Prince Zuko,” his uncle is disgusted, Zuko can hear it in his voice, “all you can dream of is your father.”

---

“I’m sorry,” Zuko muttered into the dark, turning his head onto a pillow made of fur. “‘m sorry, *sorry*.”

“Shh,” Iroh said in response.

Zuko couldn’t open his eyes, but he felt his head being lifted up slightly by gentle hands, and a cup was tilted by his mouth. He couldn’t drink it at first, as it spilled down his chin, and then he found his mouth, enough strength there, and eagerly swallowed what he could- his head ached, his body was so tired, but his *stomach* - hurt. It just hurt.

The same careful hands brought his head back down, with all the tenderness of a man holding the most delicate porcelain cup. Then Zuko’s nose tickled, and he smelled dirt and jasmine, as Iroh’s beard covered his face and a trembling mouth pressed a kiss against his forehead. There was a shout, somewhere in the distance, something loud and familiar.

“Oh, Prince Zuko,” Iroh was saying, softly, “you have…”

---

Azula wasn’t crying, just fussing. She hardly ever cried. She was different from Zuko that way, Zuko was two years older and he still cried all all the time, but not right now, not with Azula sitting between his crossed-legs, staring wide-eyed at Zuko’s scroll as he held it over her shoulders so she could see.

He was teaching her letters, trying to explain what he didn’t fully understand, as Azula squirmed on his chest and kept trying to pick up the toy Zuko had kicked away from them. “No,” Zuko chided her, frowning, as he wrapped one arm around her stomach to hold her in tighter, “you can’t play now.”

“*No*,” Azula repeated, pouting, as she raised her hand up over her head to push into Zuko’s cheek. “*No*!”

He kept his arms around her, holding the scroll closer to her face and frowned. “‘Zula,” Zuko muttered, “you’re not being right.” She tried to wiggle out again but he leaned forward, putting his head on her shoulder, and for a moment she stopped. Just looking at him. Big, golden eyes that were the same as his blinking back.

“Zuko, what are you doing?”

Memory slipped away, fading into the dark like water that trickled along a slope, growing dark with mud. Zuko watched as the world around him grew darker.

Azula was unnaturally still in his arms as she only blinked at him. She wasn’t fussing anymore, wasn’t moving, as still as the dolls she always hated. “‘Zula?” Zuko whispers. How old are they here? Three? Five?

“What are you doing?”

“I’m… teaching her,” Zuko realizes as he speaks, as he lets the scroll he was holding fall, slowly, impossibly slowly, to the ground.

“Teaching her what?”

“How to behave,” Zuko tells his mother. She must be behind him, but he cannot turn around, Azula’s eyes, wide, and blinking, won’t let him go. “*S*he ha*s* to know to behave.” He isn’t talking right, he’s little again, back when his tongue tripped just as often as his feet.

“Doesn’t she already?”

A hand falls onto his shoulder, just placed there, not a bit of strength in it.

“Doesn’t she?”

Zuko stares back into Azula’s eyes. She blinks. He doesn’t want to blink. He doesn’t want to let her go. “*S*it *s*till, pay attention, *focu*s, listen up,” Zuko is saying the words but his mouth isn’t listening to him, it’s pouring from his mind like water, “don’t wander off, be *s* till, remember what they- *s*-*s*ay.”

“Why does she need to know?”

“It’s not ea*s*y,” Zuko confesses.

“Maybe it isn’t easy for *you*.”

“It’*s* not,” Zuko says to Azula’s childish face, “not ea*s*y.”

“That’s because of *you*, Zuko,” his mother whispers into his ear, “because you aren’t normal.”

“I’m…” Zuko wants to say it, wants to defend himself, but he… he looked at Azula. Looked at her golden eyes, looked at her the way he’d *always* looked at her, jealous, even this far back, and knew he couldn’t say a word in his defense.

“If you were normal you wouldn’t make so many mistakes.”

Zuko isn’t able to speak anymore. His mother passes then, in front of him, and he realizes it never was her in the first place, it can’t be, she’s so much less real than the shade before, she looks like his mother, but her expression, the light in her eyes, everything about her was… hollow. “Come,” his not-mother says, reaching her hands out to little Azula with stiff movements like a puppet on a string, “give me your sister.”

He does, of course he does. Zuko loosens his grips and slides his hands just under his arms, lifting her only the slightest bit as not-mother picks her up the rest of the way. She raises her back, holding Azula tight to her chest.

And, coming out of the darkness as if emerging from a fog, Father steps through.

Zuko watches, unable to say a word, as his mother casually sets Azula in his father’s arms. He wants to stand, but he can’t, he’s stuck, he’s powerless, he can’t *do anything,* he can’t stop it, he can’t protect her when he can’t even protect himself, and Azula was always so much better at protecting herself, she never needed Zuko, she didn’t want him, she was fine. Father was never as harsh with her as he was to Zuko.

The not-mother stands there, passive and lifeless, *resigned*, as Father hoists Azula up in his arms and turns to walk back into the darkness of the room behind. Taking her. Leaving Zuko with his mother.

This happened before, this part was real, it was still a dream but was splashed with memory, echoing throughout every moment as Ozai walked away. Something was different now.

Azula, looking up from Ozai’s shoulder, blinked back at Zuko. Then, her child's hand trembling, raised an arm as if she was reaching for him.

As Zuko watched his father take her away, jealousy slipped from his control, bolstered at the sight of the both of them, and as it filled him in entirely it transformed into anger as clear and pure as untinted glass. Anger that continued when they left, as his mother faded, as there was no one left in the dream but him, because the focus of his anger was still there.

---

Zuko woke up with a start, his eyes flinging open and immediately regretted it. The tension that flew through his body, instantly on waking, sent shockwaves of pain into his stomach and he felt instantly sick. It was bright as well, too bright, enough that opening his eyes was nearly as much of an assault on his senses as the pain coursing around his center.

He groaned, a horrible sound from low in his throat, as his eyes watered and he forced them closed as tightly as he could.

“Oh, I didn’t think-"

“He’s awake?”

“He *shouldn’t* be, not yet. You distracted me.” That was a familiar, accusing voice, in a strange way, a way that was both comforting yet Zuko could feel his inner fire rising in response, as if preparing for a fight - and that, that, that *hurt* , as the flames gasped to life in his wounded center, as the spark of his spirit wanted to rage inside a part of him that roiled so deeply with pain. “I need that- no, *that* - where *I’m pointing*!”

Zuko gritted his teeth, grinding them against each other as he pushed his head back, neck straining into a fur covered fabric behind his head.

“Okay,” the voice said, as a soft hand pressed onto his wrist, “thanks.” She raised the other hand, up to his forehead, and then as the hand lifted away so did the sweat dripping down his neck.

*Oh*, Zuko thought, feeling utterly exhausted and horribly coherent for once, *Katara*. It was not a comforting feeling, realizing he was lying down, utterly helpless, unable even to open his eyes, as *Katara* was watching over him. He would have felt better, so much better, if he could recognize the other voice beside him but that was foreign; his heart raced, and Katara’s hand slipped to the back of his head.

“He needs to sleep *more*? How long do you think he’ll need to sleep?”

Something cool touched Zuko’s lower lip, and then, as Katara used her hand to raise his head, ever so slightly, an extremely bitter liquid trickled into his mouth, slipping between his teeth to curl his tongue. It tasted like medicine in the universal sense, and after a moment of resistance, tensing his jaw, Zuko realized it must actually be that, medicine, and forced his mouth to relax just enough to drink.

“Why?” Katara asked, sounding annoyed, “Are you going to interrogate *him* too?”

“Of course I am. And,” the stranger sighed, “I think it was more than fair I did the same for the General, I know you and your friends might have a different impression of him but-"

“I *never said* I didn’t agree,” Katara said, harshly, and her hand on the back of Zuko’s neck tightened a bit, the vial she was holding moved to dribble liquid down his neck, but she returned it quickly. Muttering under her breath.

“You implied it.”

“So?” Katara tipped the vial further, until it seemed to empty, and pulled it away.

Zuko wished he could have some water, normal water, to ease the bitterness in his mouth, but he wasn’t able to speak. Just like the dream, though this time he knew why, the combination of the tension in his body and the deep aching exhaustion in all his limbs made even the slightest motion seem like a monumental undertaking. That liquid, whatever it was, was heavy, thick, and as he felt it course down along his throat Zuko thought he might understand its purpose; medicine meant to lull him back into sleep.

“You’re very good with him,” the stranger complimented, as if several moments had passed in silence that Zuko had been too tired to notice.

“He’s a *patient*,” Katara grumbled, “I’m a healer.”

“I’m impressed.”

“I- thank you.”

“So this… really is the son of the Fire Lord?”

“Yes,” Katara said.

Despite himself, Zuko could feel the tension in his arms and jaw beginning to ease. It was gradual, accompanying a slight quieting of the pain around his stomach, as his inner fire simpered down into embers. The medicine was strong, whatever it was, certainly strong enough that he wasn’t sure Katara or the stranger knew he was awake enough to hear what they were saying.

“It’s a bit unreal,” the stranger said quietly, “to have two members of the enemy’s family so close. To see him just… sleeping.”

“He needs to sleep, he almost- he…” Katara’s voice slipped from Zuko’s grasp for a moment, too quiet for him to hear, and then, “it’s not like I *want* him here.”

“Sokka seems to,” the stranger mused. “*And* the Avatar.”

“Then ask *them*.”

“I want to know what *you* think, Katara,” his voice was kind, this stranger, this person Zuko didn’t know, a bit rhythmic too, in the way he spoke, enough that if Zuko didn’t continue to fight it he might find his voice calming enough to drift him off to sleep. “I want to- I want to hear about everything. *Anything*. I do.”

It would be easy to sleep. Pain would be easier to deal with while he was asleep but he - it wasn’t easy to let go. Not here. With Katara nearby, and a stranger. Zuko had always been a light sleeper, same as his mother, waking up at the slightest change of the light, or the quietest footfall; he wasn’t good at relaxing when he didn’t trust the people around him. When his uncle wasn’t near.

He hadn’t realized he’d tensed up his hand again until Katara’s fingers were guiding his fist apart. Then, slowly but, gently, she held his hand.

“I have a job to do,” Katara said, “I can’t let you distract me, Dad, he- he needs to sleep.”

“Alright,” the stranger said kindly, “I… alright.”

---

More dreams passed, fitfully, far more peaceful after he could feel cool water healing him, then the fever and shivers would strike again and they’d grow tumultuous. Like a storm casting fierce waves on a shore, as a helpless creature lay trapped on the sand, only finding relief in the interim between crashes of salty force. Sometimes he was that creature, pinned, waiting. Sometimes he was someone else entirely, wading through rice fields of rosey gray. For a long period of time, perhaps even a full night, Zuko was certain he was a dragon, trapped high on the ledge of a perilous mountain, his wings outstretched behind him and yet refusing to fall, despite whispers of encouragement, despite knowing better things were waiting for him above, because deep in the head of the dragon, old, harsh words still had bite, still echoed, telling the dragon if it fell it would fall, that its wings were not strong enough to fly and never would be.

---

Resting against a dying sakura tree beside a small pond, a long blue strip of torn fabric covering his eyes, Sokka looks up as Zuko approaches and smiles. Zuko tries, as he looks down at him, to recall why he’d been so determined to blindfold Sokka in the first place when the sight of him there, grinning at Zuko’s presence, could only be improved if bright blue eyes brightened as he approached.

So, as he kneels down on the manicured grass, Zuko reaches out with determined hands to pull the blindfold away; only to find he cannot. His hands are shackled.

He notices only then the fire in the distance, bright and edging closer while the two of them sit in the field as if it wasn’t even there.

Sokka, with a chuckle, brings his hands to Zuko’s, a key resting on his palm. “A spark,” Sokka mutters, his voice like a breeze, and he brought to key to Zuko’s wrists to free him, “that’s all a raging fire needs to start.”

Just a spark, just a blast of flame over a thatch roof, and then a village is up in flames. Zuko winces. He looks beyond Sokka toward the wall of fire that is coming closer, wondering why they haven’t moved, why Zuko hasn’t lifted a hand to try to stop it.

“You have to be more careful,” Sokka is saying, as the metal falls to the dirt below and Zuko is free, “have to remember where the fire should go. You have to be angry at the *right* person.”

“I’m angry at myself,” Zuko tells him quietly, “and the world, and *everything*, I- all the time.”

“Like fire.”

“Like I’m all fire,” Zuko admits to him. Of course these words come to him in the guise of *Sokka*, of everyone- there’s no one else he’s so certain he would listen to. No one else Zuko wants to think of, when he thinks of someone intelligent, someone forgiving, no other eyes he’s more curious see himself through.

“Fire that meets fire destroys itself,” Sokka tells him, his voice simple and clipped, like a lecturer, “fire can be fought with fire, but if it’s inside it might burn you up.”

“Shouldn’t it?” Zuko asks him.

“If you aimed a mirror between the sun and the source of your anger, where it all began, would the source be you?” Sokka is still blindfolded, but seeing, somehow, as he raises a finger to press against the left side of Zuko’s face. “Was it you who lit your anger? Or someone else. Where did it begin? Who *should* you be angry at?” Zuko is frozen as Sokka pulls away. “Who’s hands started the fire?”

Then Zuko is back, once again, kneeling on the tournament ground that was the scene of so many of his dreams, begging, desperate, *pleading* with the looming form of his father who is tall enough to block out the sun.

---

Waking up, as always, came to him all at once like a snap of the fingers. Zuko was awake, not quite fully as his body still ached with sleep and the desire to toss and turn but no strength to do so; it was early in the morning, so early that the majority of the world would think of it as late. Zuko could feel the sun halfway underneath him, still several hours to go before it rose.

He heard a voice shaking with both age and exhaustion, as it half sang and half hummed through an old song. It was peaceful, but strange, but then again, that’s how Zuko tended to describe his uncle in his own head.

Zuko felt better, far more awake than he’d even been last time, but he couldn’t summon any urge to open his eyes. He would rather just lie there, which, if he really let himself think about it, seemed lazy, but a somewhat kinder thought came to his mind, one that spoke with his uncle’s voice, that after he’d come so close to death it was only right to allow himself rest. Another thought, unbidden, offered up the idea that if he did try to wake he’d be worse than useless in his current state, likely unable even to hobble around with a crutch, just a burden.

Iroh’s voice hitched for a moment, and then Zuko felt a beard itching on his forearm as a hand reached out to gently lay on his wrist.

Zuko swallowed, keeping his eyes shut, wondering how long it had been since he’d moved from this position resting on his back, and then managed, barely, to remember a bit of what he’d overheard before from Katara and the stranger. Zuko didn’t know where they were, only that there were other people who didn’t trust his uncle. Who *interrogated* him.

“Are you alright?” Zuko asked. His voice was hoarse, but not weak.

That must have been a good sign, must have made Iroh happy, because he took Zuko’s wrist and lifted it to his mouth and Zuko could feel his uncle smiling against the back of his hand. “Very much so,” Iroh whispered.

“Good,” Zuko muttered. *Good*.

“How are you,” Iroh asked softly, “my nephew?”

Zuko turned his head slightly, and the fur he was lying against tickled the end of his nose. He sighed, not for any reason, just because his body wanted to. “‘M fine,” Zuko told him, “I’m alright.”

“You are,” Iroh said, and Zuko felt his uncle leaning forward as Zuko’s arm went with him. “You *are* alright,” his voice was soft, trembling, like the sound of gentle rain drizzling onto a pond. Zuko could even feel the drops of water falling, as if on his palm, and wondered if he was starting to dream again. “I am so proud of you.”

Zuko frowned, his forehead clenching tight, confused. “You are?” He asked, his throat scratching in a way that threatened to make him cough; words were muddying into each other to sound unclear, even to him, as he spoke them aloud.

“Of course I am,” Iroh said kindly. One hand reached out, which Zuko only knew when a warm thumb brushed his unscarred cheek; he grunted his annoyance instead of a response and Iroh chuckled. His uncle’s hand stayed on the side of Zuko’s face as he leaned over him.

For a while it was quiet and Zuko felt close to sleeping again, but tried to fight it off. Wanted to stay here, where it was peaceful, instead of the hurricane that waited for him in his dreams.

“I suppose it makes sense,” Iroh’s voice rumbled, soothing, “that I would be here again. Watching over you as you slept, as you healed. It was where we were when our journey together started, and now again at such a pivotal moment, you-“ his voice choked, hesitating, and continued on as if the words were a struggle to say, “It doesn’t seem *right* to me. That *every* moment- of *change*- of… *growth* for you should… leave you like this.”

“Uncle,” Zuko muttered. He felt like he should open his eyes, should say something else, but he was so *tired*. He owed Iroh apologies, he knew that, there had been a stack of debted apologies growing ever since he’d been small; slights and insults that hadn’t been meant, ones that *had*, money borrowed to fund his journey with the intent to repay only if he succeeded and now Zuko never would. He owed his uncle an apology for agreeing to let him come. Owed for embarrassing *him* too, at the war meeting, as Iroh had been the one to vouch for Zuko in the first place. Owed him for leaving twice, in almost as many months. For the lies, everything he’d withheld. For the disguise he’d worn the moment they’d arrived at the city. For taking Iroh for granted just because he *could* . “I *do*…” Zuko’s own voice was so quiet, like he couldn’t even bear to hear himself say the words, “I… love you.”

“Zuko,” Iroh said, and Zuko could feel his uncle’s smile pressed against his mouth grow wider before he lowered his hand, probably intending to talk, but Zuko wasn’t done. He had to say it, now, before health or nerves and better judgement forced the words back down again.

“I always… it’s not *easy*,” he continued quietly, pushing his face further into the furs as an uncomfortable ache built in his chest.

“It’s all right,” Iroh told him.

“No, it’s just… *you* said it, and I- never,” Zuko swallowed. Took in a ragged breath. “I think it might… be a curse. When I say it.”

He felt the bed, mattress, hammock, whatever it was he was lying on, dip under a heavy weight by his hip and he knew Iroh had sat down. And then, just a moment later, his uncle’s hand on his cheek slipped back, as coarse hair scratched on Zuko’s neck. It was all the warning he *got* , just enough for Zuko to feel heat preemptively rising onto his face, before Iroh pressed a kiss onto his forehead.

Zuko groaned, not even meaning to, and rolled his body just slightly so he could hide his face more.

Iroh laughed, full-bellied and warm, and despite *everything* , Zuko’s mouth twitched upward into a weak smile. “*Zuko.*” His uncle sat upward with a sigh, leaving his hand on the side of Zuko’s face. “I don’t believe love is a curse,” Iroh told him gently.

“You *should*,” Zuko reminded him gruffly, “considering.”

“No, not a curse. It is easy to feel that way, I admit, when grief settles in, but love can never be a curse,” Iroh told him softly, “love is what life *is*, at its heart. Loving the sun, loving the open sea, time spent with the ones you care about, those who care about you; nothing so beautiful can be a curse, Zuko. Even grief can’t spoil such a thing, over time it just grows sore, fits back into its place, and love *always* comes back. The pain is only there to remind us how deeply we once loved and were loved in return.” He brushed aside some of the wild hair on Zuko’s head, tucking it behind his ear. “And show us how greatly we will one day love again.”

Zuko grunted, as a reply.

Iroh chuckled. “Believe me, sometimes grief is far too much for a person to handle, sometimes it goes on much too long.” He sighed, softly. “There is no curse on love, Zuko, but indeed if you are cursed, all the blame comes from my family. Maybe now you’ll be free of it, since you’ve chosen to fight against my brother, to correct my own mistakes; the mistakes of your grandfather, and his father. It’s too much of a burden for you, I know, but fate is hardly fair.” Iroh paused for a moment. “Though if there is indeed a curse, then, Prince Zuko, it means there is a curse to be *broken*.”

Zuko couldn’t help opening his eyes. Though all he could see was grey fur rising into his vision, and a gray world around him so dark that despite his eyes being well adjusted, there wasn’t any color. It was at least *quiet*. Gentle in its own way from the lack of light.

“You won’t be alone,” Iroh promised him, “I’m here. It also appears you’ve managed, with some great luck, to have found yourself some friends who are quite determined to help. And the young Avatar who has a great burden of his own, that you can help in return.”

“Hm.”

“What is on your mind?” Iroh asked him.

Zuko frowned into the darkness. His uncle was warm, heavy too as his weight forced Zuko to lean in to him, and it was nice. It made being honest, it made saying what he knew he was going to say next easier. “What if a part of me… loves them,” he said quietly, “still?”

Iroh’s hand tensed for a moment. Then he sighed and seemed to relax. “Still?”

“Not the same but…” Zuko tried to think of the words, it wasn’t easy. Not now. Not when even just this conversation had him worn out and ready to sleep again. “It’s, like, it feels like a scar.”

“I see,” Iroh said thoughtfully. He was quiet for a long moment, quiet long enough Zuko’s eyes fell shut again and he started to hear some distant clanging of metal. “I believe that’s wise, Zuko.”

Zuko grimaced. “Is it?”

“Old grief, tensed over, still sore and tender,” Iroh mused. “I may have hardened my own heart but, it was never your way. You’ve always felt everything so greatly.”

“‘m angry,” Zuko mumbled.

Iroh chuckled. “Yes, even *that*. It is better to be angry than to feel nothing at all, even if the anger is intense and often misdirected; to feel *nothing* is, it’s a kind of death.” His uncle’s hand brushed over his forehead now, pushing back his hair with delicate movements. “My love for *you*, Zuko, is the *wildest* and widest of rivers.”

Zuko groaned.

“That isn’t a proverb,” Iroh said quickly, before Zuko had the chance, “more of a metaphor. Very straightforward for me, I think.”

He was right about *that*, and probably about the rest too. Zuko sighed, feeling the fur tickle across his nose and cheek as he exhaled. “Even now?” He asked.

“Especially now.”

“Even with what you know about me?”

“How could something so small stop a mighty river? If it ever was meant to try, at all?” His uncle made a noise, one that Zuko’s tired brain took awhile to recognize as a yawn. Iroh was quiet again for a long moment before continuing, in a teasing tone, “Though you must explain to me sometime how it is *that* is the boy who caught your attention.”

Zuko snorted. “He’s nicer than *Jet*,” he muttered, feeling his own yawn beginning to ache against his jaw.

Iroh chuckled again, from deep in his stomach, “He definitely is *that*, I-“ and then he paused, and a moment later said, “oh.”

“‘m tired, Uncle.”

“Ah, *yes*, well, you…” Iroh coughed. “Yes. You should sleep. Build up your strength.” And, as Zuko did feel himself beginning to fall asleep again, Iroh said in a soft voice, “Sleep well, Prince Zuko.”

---

Zuko sleeps, dreamless and deep.

---

The next time he was awake Zuko definitely wished he wasn’t.

He drummed his index fingers against his chest, by the clavicles, looking around the room he was in at literally anything besides Katara. She snapped the water above his stomach, bringing it down with a soothing glow, her motions healing and gentle but the scowl on her face anything but.

Zuko had never had much of a good look at this room. He had clouded memories of occasions where his uncle would take him to a room off in the corner that must have been a bathroom, remembered snippets of being fed some kind of soup from the table at the side of the bed, but that was all. This was the first time he was awake and coherent when the light was coming in from the open door to the hallway, light that clearly belonged to a sun.

Metal walls, metal ceiling, metal floors and a metal roof. Boxed in like a cage, unfeeling and cold, no decorations but a tattered old *Fire Nation* flag raised at his left where the wall likely met the sea. It was a warship.

And a nicer one than his old one at that, considering this must be the captain’s chambers and unlike his old one, it came with a sturdy metal bed. The unopened door on the farther wall must lead to the bathroom. There was a large desk by that, though otherwise the room was a little conspicuously bare. No rug or ornamental touches to indicate who had occupied the room previously. Where it had come from. Who lived here, before it was taken over by the en… by *them*.

Zuko drummed his fingers against his chest and blinked up at the ceiling. If Katara was sitting on his *other* side it would have been much easier to ignore her, unfortunately she’d pulled her chair up to his right.

“*H’em*,” Katara coughed. Zuko stared upward. Then, more forcefully, she *coughed* again.

Zuko forced himself to meet her eyes. She glared back. *Fuck*. He should say something, that must be why she wanted his attention, maybe thank her? For not being dead? Would that be strange? He wasn’t eager to look down at his stomach, he’d seen enough of burns on his skin, but he could feel its stiffness, how much the pain was lessened; she’d healed him, *been* healing him, which was fine to think about in the past tense but being *awake* for it was another thing altogether.

“Uh,” Zuko said. Then he paused.

Katara, her hands were still moving around his stomach and guiding the glowing light, as if what she was doing was rote to her by this point. She cocked an eyebrow at him and waited.

“Where’s Sokka?” Zuko asked.

Her jaw clenched tight, so much so Zuko could see it, and her hands stiffened as the water on his stomach paused and grew clear. Katara took a deep breath. Zuko held his. “Sokka?” She said, after a pause long enough Zuko’s chest had started pounding, “What about Sokka?” Her hands began to move again, swirling over each of her wrists in turn and calling the water back under her control.

Zuko, glad the many fur blankets on the bed propped his head and back up, leaned up on his elbows to give himself the slightest bit of lift to watch her. If she was annoyed by him sitting upright, moving his stomach an inch from where she was working on, she didn’t say anything; Katara just shot him another angry glance.

He did, apparently, end up disturbing a round, small object located by his feet. A small head poked up out of nowhere and two giant, foot-long ears shot up in the air from behind the folds of a blanket. Momo, looking back at Zuko with wide blinking eyes, hissed and then lay back down, a weight returning to Zuko’s left foot he hadn’t noticed before.

“How do I… get rid of him?” Zuko asked sourly. He’d been scratched up *plenty* by that lemur in the past, sharing a bed with it when he was barely conscious more than a few hours a day was the last thing he wanted.

Katara snorted at him. “You can’t.” She lifted her hands, pulling water up into the air from Zuko’s stomach, returning it to a bowl on the table by the bed.

“Why…” would it *want* to be there? Considering Zuko had *kidnapped* it, although, as Zuko watched a long white and brown tail twitch by his ankle, he wondered if Momo even remembered or cared. Feeding him, and just generally being a warm thing to sleep on, was probably more important to the little creature.

“*Because*,” Katara snapped, lifting a hand to her hair as if to check to be sure it was still all in place, “Aang wanted Momo to watch you.”

Zuko frowned. “How is your pet *monkey* supposed to ‘watch me’?” He asked sourly.

Katara leaned back on her chair and crossed her arms. She was tense, glaring for a moment at Momo, who had curled up to sleep and didn’t appear to notice her, before turning her storming eyes back to Zuko. “Aang just said he *felt better* if Momo was… *here*,” she said curtly.

Zuko, doing his best to swallow a groan, sat up more on the bed. He couldn’t help a quick glance downward as he did. The burn was red, but precise, covering just a bit over two inches of skin and the width of two fingers. Covering what was, Zuko knew now, far more damage to the organs underneath.

He lowered his hand to brush against the edge of it thoughtfully, where excessively tender skin met the harsh, red-raised blister that was sickeningly yellow around the edges. It looked good. Zuko could tell; with however much time had passed and the healing Katara must have done, this scar was going to be… better. At least better than what was on his face. He needed to thank her. Zuko just had to figure out where to *start*.

“He’s got some stupid idea in his head,” Katara continued, clearly angry. Her legs were crossed now too, the raised one tapping the edge of the mattress as her eyes were closed. She scowled. “That what happened was *his fault*.”

“Oh.”

“And that’s *ridiculous*,” Katara snarled, “but he thinks he could have stopped it or something, as if *he’s responsible* for having to leave his teaching with the guru to come *save* my brother. From *your* - from your…”

“Sister?” Zuko offered.

“I *know*!” She yelled, eyes flying open, sitting up for a moment just to throw her arms up in the air before she sat right back down. “It’s stupid.” Zuko was about to say something in response when Katara started up again. “And is it *so bad* that he asked Momo to watch you?! You should be grateful, do you know that? Aang *loves* Momo!”

Katara had raised an accusing finger at him and Zuko stared at it for a moment. “Okay?” He eventually said, sheepish.

“I *know* about you two,” Katara told him fiercely, “Sokka told me *everything*.”

Zuko swallowed, hard. He could feel the heat rising into his face. *You*, *what* ? He stared at her.

Now smirking, Katara met his gaze straight on and didn’t back down.

“H- how much of it?” Zuko asked, hoping he was hiding his nervousness but knowing he probably wasn’t.

“*Why*?!” She asked, leaning forward with one eyebrow raised, “You have something *else* to hide?”

“I don’t…” *Did he*? Zuko wasn’t exactly sure whether or not he *did* have, in the more serious sense of things, something to hide. The rest of it there, was, a- a *good* amount that he’d prefer never came to light. That he’d rather stayed *private*. Certainly to *her*.

“*Oh*,” Katara leaned back in the chair and crossed her arms again, “I know *all* about V-“ she shook her head, then said the word again like a curse, “*Voak*.”

Zuko was sure it was another blow to his honor when the first reaction he had to that was to be *glad*. It took him several seconds, looking at Katara, her enraged eyes staring back, before everything that that statement *meant* sunk in and he stopped feeling relief that she didn’t know the more pleasant details. Then again, maybe she *did*. Zuko didn’t know anything about how close she and Sokka might be. Was that a kind of thing siblings shared?

That really *shouldn’t* be his most pressing worry, kisses in shade, or the pastries, *that letter*, crying in front of him, or- *no*. A faded memory popped unwelcome into his head like the crash of a gong. Zuko’s eyes widened. *He called Sokka a turtleduck?!*

“Are you at least *sorry*?!” Katara demanded. Her words snapped him back to attention. “Do you regret it? *Any* of it?!”

Zuko winced. “Uh… I- *most* of it,” he admitted.

Katara stood up and glared down at him. “What do you mean *most* of it?”

“I-“ Zuko frowned. “Of course I don’t regret *everything*!”

“You should!” She shouted down at him, flinging one arm to the side. As if on reflex, like she didn’t realize she’d done it, the water in the bowl surged away and into the wall, freezing on impact. “You *should* regret all of it! You should be *sorry*!”

“I *am*,” Zuko snarled back at her, “for plenty of it, but-!”

“You’re such a- and I *saved your life*!” Katara reminded, glaring so hard at him a vein was visible in her forehead, “And you just, *lied*, and… and burn stuff!”

“I’m a *firebender*,” Zuko said angrily.

“I *know* you’re *a firebender*!” She yelled at him. Then she glared, breathing hard, looking at him with an expression of pure fury. “You just…” Katara said, the words cut off not by anything else but her rage growing strong enough to cut herself off.
